books.section: Topic 6.7 Labor in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress (August 28, 1893)

options.misconception: Wages are never named anywhere in the passage.
options.text: It lists higher wages first, before all other demands in the passage.

options.misconception: The passage says nothing about striking for pay alone.
options.text: It says unions should strike for pay alone and for nothing else.

options.misconception: Gompers asks for more schoolhouses, not for employers to fund them.
options.text: It asks employers to pay for all schooling for the workers’ children.
It lists schools, books, leisure, and justice, none of which is a wage.

rationales.A: Wages are never named anywhere in the passage, so they cannot be listed first.
rationales.B: The passage says nothing about striking, let alone striking for pay alone.
rationales.C: Gompers asks for more schoolhouses; he never says employers must pay for them.
rationales.D: Schools, books, leisure, and justice fill the list, and none of them is a wage demand.
rationales.general:
Test the claim against the whole list.
1. The claim is that Gompers wanted only higher wages.
2. Read the list: schoolhouses, books, learning, leisure, justice.
3. Not one item in the list is a wage.
4. A list with no wage in it answers a wages-only claim.
Remember: to answer an “only” claim, count what the source actually lists.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)
stem: A student claims Gompers wanted only higher wages. The passage best answers that claim in which way?

stimulus.source_note: Samuel Gompers, address to the International Labor Congress, August 28, 1893. Public domain (Samuel Gompers Papers, University of Maryland).
stimulus.text: “What does labor want? . . . We want more schoolhouses and less jails; more books and less arsenals; more learning and less vice; more constant work and less crime; more leisure and less greed; more justice and less revenge; in fact, more of the opportunities to cultivate our better natures, to make manhood more noble, womanhood more beautiful and childhood more happy and bright.”
